questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The positively charged particle found in the nucleus of an atom is called the
questions.explanation: The proton is a positively charged particle located within the atomic nucleus.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The neutral (uncharged) particle found in the nucleus of an atom, alongside protons, is called the
questions.explanation: Neutrons carry no electrical charge and, together with protons, make up the nucleus of an atom.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The negatively charged particle that orbits the nucleus of an atom, and whose movement constitutes electric current, is called the
questions.explanation: Electrons are negatively charged particles orbiting the nucleus; the directed movement of free electrons constitutes electric current.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom that are loosely bound and can move relatively freely between atoms are called
questions.explanation: Free electrons are loosely bound outer-shell electrons capable of moving between atoms, enabling the flow of electric current in conductors.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The fundamental electrical quantity representing a surplus or deficiency of electrons, measured in coulombs, is called
questions.explanation: Electric charge (Q), measured in coulombs, quantifies the surplus or deficiency of electrons possessed by a body or particle.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The rate of flow of electric charge past a given point in a circuit is called
questions.explanation: Current (I) measures the rate at which electric charge flows past a point in a circuit, conventionally measured in amperes.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The electrical quantity that represents the difference in electric potential energy between two points, driving current through a circuit, is called
questions.explanation: Voltage (potential difference) represents the energy difference per unit charge between two points, providing the 'push' that drives current.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The electrical quantity that describes a material's opposition to the flow of electric current is called
questions.explanation: Resistance (R), measured in ohms, quantifies how strongly a material opposes the flow of electric current.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The energy supplied per unit charge by a source, such as a battery, to drive current around a complete circuit is called the
questions.explanation: Electromotive force (emf) is the total energy supplied per unit charge by a source, distinct from terminal voltage, which accounts for internal losses.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Ohm's Law states that, at constant temperature, the current flowing through a conductor is
options: independent of both voltage and resistance
directly proportional to both voltage and resistance
directly proportional to the voltage across it and inversely proportional to its resistance
inversely proportional to both voltage and resistance
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law (V = IR) states that current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance, at constant temperature.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: According to Ohm's Law, if the voltage across a resistor is doubled while its resistance remains constant, the current will
questions.explanation: Since current is directly proportional to voltage (I = V/R), doubling the voltage while keeping resistance constant doubles the current.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The resistance of a conductor is generally directly proportional to its
questions.explanation: A longer conductor offers more opposition to current flow, making resistance directly proportional to length.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The resistance of a conductor is generally inversely proportional to its
questions.explanation: A conductor with a larger cross-sectional area provides more paths for current flow, reducing resistance; hence resistance is inversely proportional to area.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The property of a specific material that determines how strongly it resists the flow of electric current, independent of its physical dimensions, is called
questions.explanation: Resistivity is an intrinsic material property describing its inherent opposition to current flow, distinct from resistance which also depends on dimensions.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: For most conductors, an increase in temperature generally causes their resistance to
questions.explanation: Most metallic conductors experience increased resistance as temperature rises, due to increased atomic vibration impeding electron flow.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: In a series circuit, the current flowing through each component is
questions.explanation: In a series circuit, there is only one path for current, so the same current flows through every component.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: In a series circuit, the total resistance is calculated as
options: the product of all individual resistances
the sum of all individual resistances
always equal to the smallest individual resistance
the reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals of individual resistances
questions.explanation: Series circuit total resistance is simply the sum of each individual resistor's value, since current must pass through all of them sequentially.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is
options: the same as the total supply voltage
equal to the sum of all branch voltages
different for each branch depending on its resistance
questions.explanation: In a parallel circuit, all branches share the same voltage, equal to the total supply voltage across the parallel combination.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: In a parallel circuit, the total resistance can be calculated using the formula
options: R(total) = R1 x R2 x ... (direct product)
R(total) is always equal to the largest resistor
questions.explanation: Parallel circuit total resistance is found using the reciprocal formula, since additional parallel paths reduce the overall resistance.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The internal resistance of a battery or cell causes the terminal voltage under load to be
options: exactly equal to the cell's emf at all times
less than the cell's emf, due to the voltage drop across the internal resistance
greater than the cell's emf in every case
questions.explanation: Internal resistance causes a voltage drop within the cell itself, meaning the terminal voltage delivered to an external circuit is less than the emf when current flows.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) states that at any junction in a circuit, the
options: voltage entering the junction equals the voltage leaving it
total current entering the junction equals the total current leaving it
resistance at the junction is always zero
current is always split equally regardless of resistance
questions.explanation: KCL reflects conservation of charge, stating that current entering a junction must equal the current leaving it, with no charge accumulating.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) states that around any closed loop in a circuit, the
options: sum of all resistances equals the applied voltage
sum of the voltage drops equals the total applied voltage (emf)
sum of all currents equals zero
voltage is always the same at every point
questions.explanation: KVL reflects conservation of energy, stating that the sum of voltage drops around a closed loop must equal the total emf supplied to that loop.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Joule's Law of heating states that the heat generated in a resistor is proportional to
options: the square of the resistance alone
only the voltage applied, with no dependence on current
only the resistance, regardless of current or time
the square of the current, the resistance, and the time (H = I²Rt)
questions.explanation: Joule's Law states that heat generated equals the square of the current multiplied by resistance and time (H = I²Rt), reflecting energy dissipation in a resistor.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Electrical power can be correctly expressed using the formula
questions.explanation: Electrical power has several equivalent expressions, all derived by combining Ohm's Law with the basic power relationship P = VI.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The standard SI unit of electrical power is the
questions.explanation: Power is measured in watts, representing the rate of energy conversion or transfer (one watt equals one joule per second).

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The standard SI unit of electrical energy is the
questions.explanation: Energy is measured in joules, the fundamental SI unit representing the capacity to do work.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The unit commonly used by electricity utility companies to bill customers for energy consumption is the
questions.explanation: Utility companies bill customers in kilowatt-hours (kWh), a practical unit of energy representing one kilowatt of power used for one hour.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: If an appliance rated at 2 kW operates for 3 hours, the energy consumed is
questions.explanation: Energy in kWh is calculated as power (kW) multiplied by time (hours): 2 kW x 3 hours = 6 kWh.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The equivalent resistance of two equal resistors, each of value R, connected in parallel, is
questions.explanation: For two equal resistors R in parallel, the combined resistance is R/2, since parallel paths always reduce total resistance below the smallest individual value.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The equivalent resistance of two equal resistors, each of value R, connected in series, is
questions.explanation: For two equal resistors R in series, the total resistance is simply their sum: R + R = 2R.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: If a resistor of 10 ohms has a current of 2 amperes flowing through it, the voltage across it, according to Ohm's Law, is
questions.explanation: Using V = IR: V = 2A x 10 ohms = 20 volts.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: If a circuit has a voltage of 12 volts and a resistance of 4 ohms, the current flowing through it, according to Ohm's Law, is
questions.explanation: Using I = V/R: I = 12V / 4 ohms = 3 amperes.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A conductor's ability to allow the flow of electric current, the reciprocal of resistance, is called its
questions.explanation: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, describing how easily a conductor allows current to flow, measured in siemens.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An atom that has gained or lost one or more electrons, giving it an overall electric charge, is called an
questions.explanation: An ion is an atom (or molecule) that carries a net electric charge due to the gain or loss of electrons.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The type of material that allows electric current to flow through it easily, due to having many free electrons, is called a
questions.explanation: Conductors, such as copper and aluminium, have many free electrons available to carry electric current with little resistance.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The type of material that strongly resists the flow of electric current, used to prevent unwanted current paths, is called an
questions.explanation: Insulators, such as rubber and plastic, have very few free electrons, strongly resisting current flow and providing electrical safety and isolation.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Two resistors of 6 ohms and 3 ohms connected in parallel have a combined resistance of

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Two resistors of 6 ohms and 3 ohms connected in series have a combined resistance of
questions.explanation: In series, resistances simply add together: 6 ohms + 3 ohms = 9 ohms.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An electrical circuit that provides a complete, unbroken path for current to flow is described as a
questions.explanation: A closed circuit provides an unbroken path allowing current to flow continuously around it.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An electrical circuit in which the path for current flow has been broken, preventing current from flowing, is described as an
questions.explanation: An open circuit has a break in its path, such as an open switch or broken wire, preventing current from flowing.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The invisible lines used to represent the direction and strength of a magnetic field are called
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines visually represent the direction and relative strength of a magnetic field around a magnet or current-carrying conductor.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A magnet that retains its magnetism without requiring an electric current is called a
questions.explanation: Permanent magnets retain their magnetic properties without needing an external electric current, unlike electromagnets.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A magnet created by passing an electric current through a coil of wire, often wound around a magnetic core, is called an
questions.explanation: Electromagnets generate magnetism through electric current flowing through a coil, and lose their magnetism when the current is switched off.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A coil of wire wound in a helical shape, used to produce a strong, concentrated magnetic field when current flows through it, is called a
questions.explanation: A solenoid concentrates the magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire by winding it into a helical coil shape.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The rule used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor is called the
questions.explanation: The right-hand screw rule determines the direction of the circular magnetic field around a straight conductor, based on the direction of current flow.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The rule used to determine the direction of force (motion) experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field is called
questions.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule relates the directions of magnetic field, current, and resulting force (motion) on a current-carrying conductor, useful for motors.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Faraday's Laws of electromagnetic induction describe how a voltage (emf) is induced in a conductor when
options: there is relative motion between the conductor and a magnetic field, causing a change in magnetic flux
current flows through a purely resistive circuit only
two resistors are connected in parallel
the conductor is stationary and no magnetic field is present
questions.explanation: Faraday's Laws state that an emf is induced in a conductor whenever it experiences a changing magnetic flux, such as through relative motion within a magnetic field.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Lenz's Law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it
options: reinforces and strengthens the change in magnetic flux
has no relationship to the inducing magnetic flux
flows only in direct current circuits
opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it
questions.explanation: Lenz's Law reflects conservation of energy, stating that induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the very change in flux that created it.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The phenomenon in which a changing current in a coil induces an emf within that same coil is called
questions.explanation: Self-induction occurs when a coil's own changing current induces an emf within itself, opposing the change (as per Lenz's Law).

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The phenomenon in which a changing current in one coil induces an emf in a nearby, separate coil is called
questions.explanation: Mutual induction occurs when a changing current in one coil induces an emf in a separate, nearby coil, the principle underlying transformers.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An alternating current (AC) is generally characterised by a current or voltage that
options: remains at a fixed, unchanging value at all times
periodically reverses direction, typically following a sinusoidal waveform
cannot be generated using rotating machinery
flows only in one constant direction
questions.explanation: AC is characterised by current or voltage that regularly reverses direction, commonly following a smooth sinusoidal pattern over time.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The maximum instantaneous value reached by an alternating voltage or current during a cycle is called its
questions.explanation: The peak value is the highest instantaneous magnitude reached by an AC waveform during each cycle.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The value of an alternating current that would produce the same heating effect as an equivalent direct current is called its
questions.explanation: The rms value represents the equivalent DC value that would produce the same heating (power) effect as the alternating waveform.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: For a pure sine wave, the relationship between the rms value and the peak value is given by
questions.explanation: For a sinusoidal waveform, the rms value equals the peak value divided by the square root of two (approximately 0.707 times the peak value).

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The number of complete cycles of an alternating waveform occurring per second is called its
questions.explanation: Frequency, measured in hertz (Hz), describes how many complete AC cycles occur every second.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The time taken to complete one full cycle of an alternating waveform is called its
questions.explanation: The period is the time duration of a single complete cycle of an AC waveform, and is the reciprocal of frequency (T = 1/f).

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: In a purely resistive AC circuit, the current and voltage waveforms are
options: 90 degrees out of phase, with voltage leading
90 degrees out of phase, with current leading
questions.explanation: In a purely resistive circuit, current and voltage reach their peaks and zero points simultaneously, meaning they are in phase.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current
options: lags behind the voltage by 90 degrees
is always zero regardless of voltage
is exactly in phase with the voltage
questions.explanation: In a purely inductive circuit, the current lags the applied voltage by a quarter cycle (90 degrees) due to the inductor's opposition to changing current.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current
options: lags behind the voltage by 90 degrees
is exactly in phase with the voltage
is always zero regardless of voltage
questions.explanation: In a purely capacitive circuit, the current leads the applied voltage by a quarter cycle (90 degrees) as the capacitor charges and discharges.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The total opposition to current flow in an AC circuit, combining both resistance and reactance, is called
questions.explanation: Impedance (Z) represents the total opposition to AC current flow, combining both resistive and reactive components in an AC circuit.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The power factor of an AC circuit describes the
options: ratio of real (useful) power to apparent power in the circuit
frequency of the AC supply only
total resistance of the circuit only
total inductance of the circuit only
questions.explanation: Power factor indicates how effectively an AC circuit converts supplied (apparent) power into real, useful power, influenced by the phase relationship between current and voltage.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Around a current-carrying straight conductor, the magnetic field lines form a pattern of
options: straight parallel lines along the conductor
a single line directly through the conductor
questions.explanation: The magnetic field produced by a straight current-carrying conductor forms concentric circles centred on the conductor, as described by the right-hand screw rule.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Within a solenoid carrying current, the magnetic field produced closely resembles that of a
options: bar magnet, with distinct north and south poles
questions.explanation: A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field pattern very similar to that of a bar magnet, complete with distinct north and south poles.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Like magnetic poles (for example, two north poles) placed near each other will
options: have no effect on each other
questions.explanation: Like magnetic poles repel one another, while unlike poles (north and south) attract, a fundamental property of magnetism.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Unlike magnetic poles (a north pole and a south pole) placed near each other will
options: cancel out completely with no field remaining
have no effect on each other
questions.explanation: Unlike magnetic poles attract one another, a fundamental principle underlying the behaviour of magnets.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The strength of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid can generally be increased by
options: using thicker insulation on the wire only
increasing the current or the number of turns in the coil
decreasing the current flowing through it
questions.explanation: A solenoid's magnetic field strength increases with greater current and a greater number of coil turns, and can be further boosted with a suitable magnetic core.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A step-up transformer is designed to
options: decrease the voltage from primary to secondary winding
increase the voltage from primary to secondary winding
keep the voltage exactly the same on both windings
questions.explanation: A step-up transformer has more turns on its secondary winding than its primary, increasing the output voltage relative to the input.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A step-down transformer is designed to
options: decrease the voltage from primary to secondary winding
keep the voltage exactly the same on both windings
increase the voltage from primary to secondary winding
questions.explanation: A step-down transformer has fewer turns on its secondary winding than its primary, decreasing the output voltage relative to the input.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Transformers rely fundamentally on the principle of
options: self-induction within a single isolated coil only
mutual induction between the primary and secondary windings
permanent magnetism with no changing current
questions.explanation: Transformers operate through mutual induction, where a changing current in the primary winding induces a voltage in the separate secondary winding.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A typical household electricity supply frequency in many countries, including Nigeria, is
questions.explanation: Nigeria and many other countries use a standard AC supply frequency of 50 Hz, though some countries (such as the United States) use 60 Hz.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A wiring system in which cables are run visibly along the surface of walls and ceilings, typically clipped in place, is called
questions.explanation: Surface wiring runs cables visibly along walls or ceilings, clipped directly to the surface rather than concealed within it.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A wiring system in which cables are protected and routed through rigid or flexible tubes, either plastic or metallic, is called
questions.explanation: Conduit wiring routes cables through protective tubing (PVC or metallic), offering mechanical protection and a route for future rewiring.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A wiring system using rectangular ducting, often used to carry multiple cables together along a common route, is called a
questions.explanation: Trunking systems use rectangular ducting to carry and organise multiple cables together along shared routes, common in commercial installations.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A switch that controls a light or circuit from only one location is called a
questions.explanation: A one-way switch simply turns a circuit on or off from a single control point.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A switch designed to work in pairs, allowing a light to be controlled from two separate locations (such as the top and bottom of a staircase), is called a
questions.explanation: Two-way switches are wired in pairs, enabling control of the same light from two different switch locations.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A switch used together with two-way switches to allow control of a light from three or more locations is called an
questions.explanation: Intermediate switches are added between two two-way switches, extending control of a circuit to three or more separate switching locations.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A fixed point in a wiring installation, fitted with contacts, into which a plug is inserted to connect an appliance is called a
questions.explanation: A socket outlet provides the connection point where a plug is inserted to supply power to an appliance.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The point in an electrical installation where the main supply is divided into separate circuits, each protected by its own fuse or breaker, is called the
questions.explanation: The distribution board (consumer unit) divides the incoming supply into individual circuits, each with its own protective device.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A safety device containing a thin wire designed to melt and break the circuit when current exceeds a safe level is called a
questions.explanation: A rewireable fuse contains a thin fuse wire that melts (breaks) when current exceeds a safe level, requiring the wire to be replaced after operation.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A safety device consisting of a sealed unit containing a fuse element, replaced as a complete unit when it operates, is called a
questions.explanation: A cartridge fuse is a sealed, factory-made unit that must be replaced entirely once it has operated, unlike a rewireable fuse whose wire alone is replaced.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A fuse specifically designed to safely interrupt very high fault currents without shattering or causing further damage is called a
questions.explanation: HBC (high-breaking-capacity) fuses are designed to safely interrupt very high fault currents, an important safety feature in higher-power installations.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A resettable protective switch that automatically trips to disconnect a circuit when current exceeds a preset safe level is called a
questions.explanation: An MCB automatically trips (switches off) when current exceeds a safe threshold, and can simply be reset once the fault is cleared, unlike a fuse which must be replaced.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A protective device that disconnects a circuit upon detecting a small leakage of current to earth, protecting against electric shock, is called an
questions.explanation: An ELCB (or modern RCD) detects small current leakages to earth, which can indicate a fault posing a shock hazard, and rapidly disconnects the circuit for safety.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The purpose of earthing an electrical installation is primarily to
options: eliminate the need for any circuit protection devices
provide a safe path for fault current, reducing the risk of electric shock
reduce the total resistance of all circuits equally
increase the overall voltage of the supply
questions.explanation: Earthing provides a low-resistance path for fault current to flow safely to earth, helping protective devices operate quickly and reducing shock risk.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: The overall resistance of the complete earth fault current path, from the point of fault back to the source, is called the
questions.explanation: Earth loop impedance must be sufficiently low to ensure enough fault current flows to operate protective devices quickly during a fault.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A measuring instrument that uses the interaction between two pieces of soft iron, magnetised by the current being measured, is called a
questions.explanation: Moving-iron instruments use the mutual repulsion or attraction of soft iron pieces magnetised by the measured current, suitable for both AC and DC measurement.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A measuring instrument that uses a coil suspended in a permanent magnetic field, deflecting in proportion to the current flowing through it, is called a
questions.explanation: Moving-coil instruments use a coil in a fixed magnetic field, deflecting proportionally to current, and are generally used for DC measurement.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An instrument specifically designed to measure electric current in a circuit is called an
questions.explanation: An ammeter measures the current flowing through a circuit, and is connected in series with the circuit being tested.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An instrument specifically designed to measure the potential difference (voltage) between two points is called a
questions.explanation: A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points, and is connected in parallel across the component being tested.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An instrument specifically designed to measure electrical resistance is called an
questions.explanation: An ohmmeter directly measures the resistance of a component or circuit, typically using its own internal power source.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An instrument specifically designed to measure electrical power consumed in a circuit is called a
questions.explanation: A wattmeter measures electrical power directly, typically combining current and voltage sensing within a single instrument.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A versatile electrical instrument capable of measuring voltage, current, and resistance, selectable via a single device, is called a
questions.explanation: A multimeter combines the functions of an ammeter, voltmeter, and ohmmeter into a single versatile instrument, selectable by a mode switch or dial.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An ammeter's measuring range can typically be extended to measure larger currents by connecting a
options: capacitor in parallel with the meter movement
shunt resistor in parallel with the meter movement
multiplier resistor in series with the meter movement
inductor in series with the meter movement
questions.explanation: A shunt resistor, connected in parallel with the ammeter's sensitive meter movement, diverts most of the current, extending the instrument's measurable range.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A voltmeter's measuring range can typically be extended to measure larger voltages by connecting a
options: inductor in parallel with the meter movement
multiplier resistor in series with the meter movement
shunt resistor in parallel with the meter movement
capacitor in series with the meter movement
questions.explanation: A multiplier resistor, connected in series with the voltmeter's meter movement, allows the instrument to measure a wider range of voltages safely.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An ammeter is always connected in a circuit in
options: series with the component whose current is being measured
no fixed configuration, as position does not matter
series with the supply neutral only, never the component
parallel with the component whose current is being measured
questions.explanation: An ammeter must be connected in series so that the entire circuit current flows through it, allowing an accurate current measurement.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: A voltmeter is always connected in a circuit in
options: series with the component whose voltage is being measured
parallel with the component whose voltage is being measured
no fixed configuration, as position does not matter
parallel with the supply neutral only, never the component
questions.explanation: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel across the component being measured, so it reads the potential difference without significantly altering the circuit's current.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An ideal ammeter should have
options: very high internal resistance, to block most of the current
very low internal resistance, to minimise its effect on the circuit being measured
no relationship between its resistance and circuit accuracy
questions.explanation: An ideal ammeter has very low internal resistance so that inserting it in series barely affects the circuit's normal current flow.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: An ideal voltmeter should have
options: no relationship between its resistance and circuit accuracy
very high internal resistance, to draw minimal current from the circuit being measured
very low internal resistance, to draw as much current as possible
questions.explanation: An ideal voltmeter has very high internal resistance so that connecting it in parallel draws minimal current, avoiding disturbance to the circuit being measured.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: PVC conduit is often preferred over metallic conduit in certain wiring installations mainly because it
options: conducts electricity better than metallic conduit
is non-conductive and resistant to corrosion
requires no earthing considerations at all in any installation
is always more expensive than metallic conduit
questions.explanation: PVC conduit's non-conductive, corrosion-resistant properties make it a popular and cost-effective choice for many wiring installations.

questions.subject: Basic Electricity
questions.text: Metallic conduit, when used in a wiring installation, should generally be properly earthed mainly because it
options: is electrically conductive and could become dangerously live if a fault occurs
is used purely for decorative purposes
never carries any risk of becoming electrically live
eliminates the need for any other protective devices in the circuit
questions.explanation: Since metallic conduit conducts electricity, it must be properly earthed so that, in the event of an internal fault, it cannot become a dangerous, unexpectedly live surface.
